We enjoy working together, developing creative ideas, and solving real-world problems. summary: Our software continuously monitors an astronaut’s biological signals, detecting deviations from normal ranges that may indicate medical conditions. It provides an initial health assessment and suggests appropriate treatment plans from its internal database, following relevant HSRB protocols. The application addresses prevention, diagnosis, and treatment, with a primary focus on prevention.
details:
Restoring a person’s health requires access to appropriate treatment and equipment. But what happens in the case of astronauts, who must stay healthy in harsh conditions with limited access to specialized medical personnel, medical supplies, and equipment? Our application, “Ophius”, aims to fill this gap. It is a decision-support system that enables continuous monitoring of astronauts' biometric indicators, along with assessment of changes in them and recommended methods to address those changes. Its primary focus is prevention, aiming to identify early deviations from normal values before symptoms develop.

More specifically, before the mission, JSON files are created for each astronaut, containing their detailed medical history and the normal values of their biological indicators. These files serve as reference points for evaluating astronauts’ health throughout the mission. During the mission, the application can receive data from compatible biosignal sensors, with the potential for integration into a space suit. For indicators whose values are obtained through specific tests, rather than biosignals, such as blood markers, the application can store the corresponding test results obtained inside the spacecraft. New biosignal and biometric values are then entered into the application through JSON files or supported sensor inputs and compared with the pre-loaded medical data. The new readings are rated as “Within limits”, “Caution”, or “Critical”. Moreover, when cardiac emergency criteria are met, an “Emergency” alert is displayed. For values outside the limits, the application suggests treatment options based on HSRB documentation and medical literature from PubMed for simpler conditions.

The application was developed using Python, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, SQLite, JSON, and PySide6/Qt. It can operate locally without requiring an internet connection for routine monitoring. During development, our team used NASA’s HSRB documentation as a guiding framework, taking into account its medical requirements, guidelines, and limitations. We also considered NASA’s Design Reference Missions (DRMs) and Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs).The treatment-support component has been implemented, while the prevention component is currently at an initial stage and requires additional data and validation.
